entries.seminar_title: Political Turnover and Fatal Government Transitions
entries.speaker: Helena Arruda
entries.abstract: Can political turnover and government transitions, though transitory, have lasting impacts on development outcomes? We hypothesize that such effects may arise when transitions coincide with critical periods for human development. Using monthly administrative data from Brazilian municipalities and adopting an event study around close elections design for identification, we find that turnover leads to sharp but temporary declines in primary healthcare provision. Prenatal consultations fall by 8.5% relative to baseline, with disruptions concentrated just around the transition months. We then estimate a model that links birth outcomes and infant mortality rates to gestational timing of exposure. We find that exposure during the second trimester of gestation is associated with lower birth weight, reduced total number of prenatal consultations during gestation. We document an increase of 1.1 total deaths and 1.3 preventable deaths per 1,000 live births. These effects manifest after the new administration takes office but reflect exposure to institutional instability during gestation. We further show that municipal personnel dismissals, especially among high-level healthcare workers, increase significantly during the transition window and precede the collapse in service delivery. Together, the results highlight how even short-lived political transitions can generate meaningful and unequal consequences when they intersect with sensitive periods of human development.

entries.speaker: Ritsu Kitagawa
entries.abstract: We test for the presence of a "daughter effect" in workplace supervisor behavior, by examining whether fathering a daughter alters how male supervisors shape the career trajectories of their female subordinates relative to their male subordinates. Using personnel records from a large Japanese manufacturer, we exploit exogenous variation in the gender of supervisors' firstborn children, coupled with periodic personnel rotations that reassign supervisors to new sets of subordinates. Comparing male supervisors whose firstborn is female to those whose firstborn is male, we find no evidence that treatment differentially favors female employees relative to male. Across promotion rates, subjective evaluations, and salary, all estimates are bounded near zero and robust to a wide range of specifications and estimation methods.  Our 95% confidence intervals mostly exclude the effect sizes predicted by LLM-simulated experts informed by the existing literature, which suggests that our null results are informative. We discuss why the daughter effect, well-documented in political and executive settings, does not extend to the routine personnel decisions of middle managers.
